title: Coal Creek Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Coal Creek wells have a 300-foot median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $25,500-$42,000 in fractured mountain bedrock.
h1: Coal Creek, Colorado Well and Drilling Guide
intro_html:
Buying land around Coal Creek means dealing with mountain bedrock, variable well depths, and a water supply that depends on the lot. Records within five miles include 3,746 permitted wells, with most serving households.

The local record is useful for setting expectations, but it does not guarantee what a new well will produce. Neighboring wells can show the likely depth, water level, and yield for an area. A driller still needs to evaluate access, geology, casing, grout, and the proposed well location.

sections.heading: Coal Creek well depth reflects fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near Coal Creek is 300 feet. The middle half runs from 165 to 452 feet, so a driller’s bid based only on the median can miss a meaningful part of the local range. The 90th-percentile depth is 650 feet, and the deepest record reaches 1,725 feet.

Depths are spread across the area: 11% are under 100 feet, 38% fall from 100 to 300 feet, 37% from 300 to 600 feet, and 14% are 600 feet or deeper. Most permits name unnamed fractured bedrock. A few identify fractured crystalline or fractured granite aquifers, while no local records identify Denver Basin aquifers.

sections.heading: What Coal Creek wells produce
sections.html:
Among the 1,188 local records that report a pump yield, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 4.0 to 9.0 gallons per minute. That is a workable range for many household wells, but yield and storage are not the same thing: a pressure tank and cistern strategy may matter on a lower-producing well.

Only 3% of reported wells produce under 1 gallon per minute. Another 25% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, 64% between 5 and 15, and 8% exceed 15. The yield figures are reported results, not a promise for an unbuilt well, especially in fractured granite or gneiss.

sections.heading: Water levels near Coal Creek and the longer record
sections.html:
Of the local records that report static water level, the median depth to water is 60 feet below the surface. The middle half is 28 to 118 feet. That range affects pump setting, well construction, trenching, and the amount of lift the system must handle.

The decade pattern suggests water levels were deeper in the more recent measurements: the median was 27 feet in the 1960s, 45 in the 1970s, 40 in the 1980s, 82 in the 2010s, and 80 in the 2020s. This is a useful regional signal, not proof that every Coal Creek parcel has a declining water table. Local elevation, fractures, recharge, and measurement conditions can change the result.

sections.heading: Coal Creek permit history and drilling records
sections.html:
Permit activity is strongest in the older development periods. Records show 51 permits in the 1950s, 197 in the 1960s, 896 in the 1970s, 530 in the 1980s, 661 in the 1990s, 444 in the 2000s, 194 in the 2010s, and 147 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most frequently recorded drillers are Ground Water Systems Inc (Wilson, Richard R.) with 568 records, James Drilling Company (Keaton, Michael K.) with 263, and Norris & Sons (Norris, T A) with 243. These records help identify local experience, but confirm current licensing, availability, and scope directly before hiring.

sections.heading: What a new Coal Creek well costs
sections.html:
Coal Creek drilling is priced around fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The local cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 300-foot median depth, drilling the hole alone works out to about $19,500 to $30,000.

A finished system, including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work, is modeled at about $25,500 to $42,000. That is a planning range, not a fixed quote. Depth, access for the rig, casing and grout requirements, difficult fractures, power distance, and site layout can move the price. Ask for separate line items so a bid can be compared with neighboring quotes.

sections.heading: Coal Creek risks to investigate before closing
sections.html:
Low yield and dry holes are the main geological risks in fractured bedrock. A nearby productive well does not prove that the same fracture crosses your parcel. Review neighboring permits, reported depths, yields, static levels, and construction details before buying. Also confirm the permit’s allowed household use and any pumping limits that apply.

Water quality deserves a separate check. Within about 10 miles are 24 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1,158 historic mine features, and 17 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped sites do not establish contamination at a particular home, but they support testing for the conditions relevant to the parcel. Keep septic setbacks, well access, drainage, and building location coordinated from the start.

sections.heading: A practical Coal Creek plan for buyers and builders
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado DWR permit records for the closest neighboring wells, then have a licensed driller review the depth and yield pattern before you make a final site decision. The local median is 300 feet, but the 165-to-452-foot middle range shows why a single depth allowance is not enough for a bid.

For a building lot, verify the well permit path, household use, septic design, driveway access, and electrical route together. A well producing 7.0 gallons per minute may be adequate, while a lower-yield result can require storage planning. Test existing water where available, inspect casing and grout records, and budget for the finished-system range rather than drilling alone.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Coal Creek, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within five miles of Coal Creek is 300 feet. The middle half runs from 165 to 452 feet. About 14% are 600 feet or deeper, and the deepest record is 1,725 feet. Fractured mountain bedrock makes parcel-to-parcel results variable, so nearby permits are more useful than the median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Coal Creek?
faq.a: The local drilling model is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 300-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $19,500 to $30,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $25,500 to $42,000. Access, depth, casing, grout, and site layout can change the final quote.

faq.q: How much water do Coal Creek wells produce?
faq.a: Among local wells reporting pump yield, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 4.0 to 9.0. About 3% report under 1 gallon per minute. These are recorded results, not guarantees. Fractured-bedrock wells can vary sharply between nearby parcels, so review neighboring yields and plan storage if the result is low.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Coal Creek, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from the well map alone. Within about 10 miles are 24 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1,158 historic mine features, and 17 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not prove a parcel is affected. Test the actual well, especially for contaminants relevant to nearby mine or cleanup history, and maintain the well and septic system.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Coal Creek?
faq.a: The reported median static water level was 27 feet below surface in the 1960s and 80 feet in the 2020s, with 82 feet in the 2010s. That pattern suggests deeper recent measurements, but it does not prove uniform decline at every parcel. Only 167 local records report static water levels, and elevation, geology, and measurement conditions affect comparisons.
